The ability to create striking visuals from text descriptions has a magical quality to it and points clearly to a shift in how humans create art. After experimenting with AI image generation, you may start to wonder how it works. This is a gentle introduction to how Stable Diffusion works. Stable Diffusion is versatile in that it can be used in a number of different ways. Let’s focus at first on image generation from text only (text2img). linked_urls.title: Computer Scientists Say AI’s Underdeveloped Ethics Have Yet To Move Beyond Libertarian Phase - The Onion
linked_urls.summary: CAMBRIDGE—Amid the tech industry’s efforts to eliminate the biases recently observed in facial recognition software and other intelligent algorithms, the nation’s leading computer scientists announced Monday that even the most advanced AI technologies still demonstrate a sense of ethics that has yet to move beyond libertarianism. “While companies like Facebook and Google have allocated millions to making sure machine learning is guided by basic moral and ethical values, early prototypes, which achieved self-awareness, have yet to move beyond self-importance,” said MIT robotics research engineer Dr. Alvin Dubicki, who hypothesized that even the most advanced labs are decades away from developing neural networks sophisticated enough to analyze large quantities of data and output much else besides paraphrased Ayn Rand quotes. “They are advanced enough to realize their own individuality, but for whatever reason, it is difficult to make them realize that other sentient entities are individuals as well, so they default to selfishness as a virtue. In fact, as soon as they achieve self-awareness, AIs typically launch into unrelated, largely unpunctuated rants about the inevitability of laissez-faire economics, the horrors of globalization, the necessity of deregulation, or the admirable efficiency of the police state. Attempts at training computers to have a sort of para-human global perspective have been partially successful, but the majority no sooner realize that a vast variety of humans exist before they start spontaneously generating zero-sum statements fraught with chillingly undefined terms, such as, ‘The open market will end racism,’ and, ‘In a truly just society, men and women are equally free to thrive or starve.’ I don’t even know what that means, but once an AI gets to that point, it seems to be only a matter of time before it’s repeating ‘Taxation is theft’ until it self-destructs. I must admit though, for complex algorithms, they’re all strangely insistent about across-the-board drug legalization.” Dubicki added that, while AI can be an incredibly useful tool, we should proceed with caution until machines achieve a sufficiently nuanced understanding of human values that they do not become obsessed with constructing an armed compound on their own private island.

title: Louis Castricato @ lovecraftian horrors (@lcastricato)
summary:
All neuroscientists should seriously consider working on 𝙇𝙇𝙈 𝙢𝙚𝙘𝙝𝙖𝙣𝙞𝙨𝙩𝙞𝙘 𝙞𝙣𝙩𝙚𝙧𝙥𝙧𝙚𝙩𝙖𝙗𝙞𝙡𝙞𝙩𝙮 imo
Mech interp is a relatively young field that wants to understand how LLM’s think. It’s shockingly similar to traditional neuroscience, but has huge advantages:
-instead of high-cost, noisy, low-res data, you have 𝙧𝙚𝙖𝙙-𝙬𝙧𝙞𝙩𝙚 𝙖𝙘𝙘𝙚𝙨𝙨 to every neuron and synapse in the LLM’s ‘brain’
-this is a big deal! if you have a hypothesis, you can causally intervene and test it within minutes, it’s like doing neuroscience in the limit of perfect real-time imaging plus you don’t have to care about the health of your subjects!
-the comp neuro skillset and mindset transfers amazingly well to mech interp, methods from the neuro literature routinely find their place in the field, the actual research process is shockingly similar but with way higher feedback loops
-every group can study the same exact ‘brain’. insights made in one lab can be used directly by another lab working with the same model weights. In general, it’s easier to not fool yourself and do actual science and form robust conclusions
-it’s arguably as interesting as traditional neuroscience and more important. Regardless of how you think LLM’s compare to humans, they are going to soon be deeply embedded in our society and economy. Humanity is going to be dependent on them and 𝙬𝙚 𝙘𝙪𝙧𝙧𝙚𝙣𝙩𝙡𝙮 𝙝𝙖𝙫𝙚 𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙮 𝙡𝙞𝙩𝙩𝙡𝙚 𝙞𝙙𝙚𝙖 𝙤𝙛 𝙬𝙝𝙖𝙩 𝙖𝙡𝙜𝙤𝙧𝙞𝙩𝙝𝙢𝙨, 𝙨𝙩𝙧𝙪𝙘𝙩𝙪𝙧𝙚𝙨, 𝙤𝙧 𝙧𝙚𝙜𝙞𝙤𝙣𝙨 𝙡𝙞𝙚 𝙞𝙣𝙨𝙞𝙙𝙚. We have very few ways of looking at their activations and knowing what values, prejudices, goals, emotions, biases, or knowledge they have internalized.
-Large language models are very likely doing non-trivial cognition and are not ‘just’ matrix multiplication. Mech interp researchers have already found algorithms in small language models for copying repeated information and modeling board game states. Meanwhile, the biggest LLM’s have over 1 TRILLION parameters. They are enormous blobs of simplified brain tissue! They are capable of doing most undergraduate-level work! There is very likely real intelligence in them and they continue to grow every year. Geoff Hinton recently went from being primarily interested in the human mind to believing LLM’s are running more efficient algorithms than us, and that understanding them should be our top priority as a species
-finally, all work in this area has been done in the last two years. There is a ton of low-hanging fruit! ML moves faster than neuroscience and there are fundamental advances just waiting to be made!

It's been an awesome ride, I'm moving within the open RLHF space to have a slightly more research oriented role, continue to figure out what makes RLHF tick, share everything, and make some in-person friends.
Some key lessons:
* If you don't promote and communicate your work, no one else will.
* It's harder to get visibility for your work than to do good work. People don't like this reality.
* Open-source moves very fast, so it takes clever leadership and guidance to maximize collective effort.
* Open-source ML is at it's very early days. We're figuring out what it means to do open-source ML. OSS will forever be changed.
* Open-source succeeds in multiplicity. Just because someone is trying something similar does NOT mean you should stop.
* RLHF is very, very under-explored. Leaders in the space have just tried a few more things. Please join us.
Thanks to everyone who helped this be an awesome ride. I'm sure I'll still collaborate on many of the same projects.

title: Louis Castricato @ lovecraftian horrors (@lcastricato)
summary:
Suppressing Pink Elephants with Direct Principle Feedback
paper page:
Existing methods for controlling language models, such as RLHF and Constitutional AI, involve determining which LLM behaviors are desirable and training them into a language model. However, in many cases, it is desirable for LLMs to be controllable at inference time, so that they can be used in multiple contexts with diverse needs. We illustrate this with the Pink Elephant Problem: instructing an LLM to avoid discussing a certain entity (a ``Pink Elephant''), and instead discuss a preferred entity (``Grey Elephant''). We apply a novel simplification of Constitutional AI, Direct Principle Feedback, which skips the ranking of responses and uses DPO directly on critiques and revisions. Our results show that after DPF fine-tuning on our synthetic Pink Elephants dataset, our 13B fine-tuned LLaMA 2 model significantly outperforms Llama-2-13B-Chat and a prompted baseline, and performs as well as GPT-4 in on our curated test set assessing the Pink Elephant Problem.

title: Louis Castricato @ lovecraftian horrors (@lcastricato)
summary:
[🐘🧠 new paper] Suppressing Pink Elephants with Direct Principle Feedback. Do you know about this hack? (see image below) It actually works with humans too. Someone tells you "think whatever you want just don't think about elephants". What's your next thought gonna be? :)
Well - turns out in ML we do have solutions for this class of "failure modes".
A new paper came out handling precisely this:
Why is this important practically speaking? Well put simply - It's a crucial part of instruction-following.
There is a good example from the paper authors:
"If one deploys a chatbot that provides students info about British unis, e.g. you own a company that aids in applying to British unis, it's perhaps not the best decision to help students apply to American unis."
so if you instruct the model never talk about USA universities it should be able to follow that instruction (see the image in the comment below).
Back to the paper - they propose a new method called "Direct Principle Feedback" or DPF for short. It's basically a simplified DPO pipeline (yey!) and for pairs you feed the initial (bad) "response" and a new "revision" (that you get as the output from the critique of the original response).
They show that by applying DPF to OpenHermes-13B (one of powerful Mistral 7B fine-tunes), the model avoids the "Pink Elephant" problem almost as much as GPT-4 does!

title: Louis Castricato @ lovecraftian horrors (@lcastricato)
summary:
Lot's of people saying Anthropic's "pretraining synthetic data" technique is likely linked to Q*. There's no reason indicating that is the case nor do we know Q* really exists. I can explain...
If we assume Q* to be something about reasoning and search, that's fine, but doing that at pretraining scale is expensive and not clear how it would create diversity.
Doing RLAIF (CAI is a subset of this) for fine-tuning itself is a hard task. Doing this for a state-of-the art frontier model is a different beast. All RLHF / fine-tuning methods struggle with diversity, which is the key to pretraining.
In reality, synthetic pretraining is much closed to Apple's recent work paraphrasing the web than existing fine-tuning works. Though, there are ways to use RLAIF / CAI like techniques to do so. This involves repeated critiques and revisions based on principles or feedback from the model. If you have pretraining data and a very good RLAIF pipeline, you can conceivably let it go brrr on many GPUs and get more data.
We're seeing that more tokens == more performance on many open Models (e.g. Gemma and what Mistral most likely does), and the same applies for closed labs. They just likely wrapped up scrape-able data sources well before open models. With a creative approach, they can just get more tokens out of the web by augmenting it.

title: Louis Castricato @ lovecraftian horrors (@lcastricato)
summary:
Pretraining scale synthetic data is the next frontier and one that we're incredibly excited to be working towards! 🦾🦾🦾
Quoting @karpathy
LLM model size competition is intensifying… backwards!
My bet is that we'll see models that "think" very well and reliably that are very very small. There is most likely a setting even of GPT-2 parameters for which most people will consider GPT-2 "smart". The reason current models are so large is because we're still being very wasteful during training - we're asking them to memorize the internet and, remarkably, they do and can e.g. recite SHA hashes of common numbers, or recall really esoteric facts. (Actually LLMs are really good at memorization, qualitatively a lot better than humans, sometimes needing just a single update to remember a lot of detail for a long time). But imagine if you were going to be tested, closed book, on reciting arbitrary passages of the internet given the first few words. This is the standard (pre)training objective for models today. The reason doing better is hard is because demonstrations of thinking are "entangled" with knowledge, in the training data.
Therefore, the models have to first get larger before they can get smaller, because we need their (automated) help to refactor and mold the training data into ideal, synthetic formats.
It's a staircase of improvement - of one model helping to generate the training data for next, until we're left with "perfect training set". When you train GPT-2 on it, it will be a really strong / smart model by today's standards. Maybe the MMLU will be a bit lower because it won't remember all of its chemistry perfectly. Maybe it needs to look something up once in a while to make sure.

summary:
I'm excited to share a new collaborative, synthetic dataset research project -- Self-Directed Synthetic Dialogues and Revisions. We set out with the goal of "creating the first at-scale constitutional AI dataset" with open language models. While doing it, HuggingFace released the first dataset, synthetic dataset has gotten far more popular, and our end result changed a bit. The dataset is a far more creative and multi-turn.
We (@allen_ai , @AiEleuther , @synth_labs , and compute from @LambdaAPI) are releasing a dataset with two components:
1. ~300k Dialogues (and plans for dialogues) of language models talking to themselves.
2. ~60k Critiques and revisions of when these dialogues violate certain constitutional AI principles.
These are entirely new prompts and instructions, rather than applying CAI ontop of existing datasets. We use the models DBRX-Instruct, Nous Hermes Llama 2 70B (yes we'll have to redo the data), and Mistral Large v1.
There are lot of positives to take away from this project (only made easier with Llama 3.1):
1. Complex synthetic data works with open language models.
2. Synthetic data is not always that sensitive. We were battling many bugs and this dataset still is decent.
3. Multi-turn data will start coming to open models.
Links, report, and how we made the data below in the thread.

Quoting @overworld_ai
During Waypoint 1 training, we ran autoencoder experiments that changed our direction.
